items.stem: Mateo records the type of transport used to get to school. What type of data is this?

items.stem: Leila is planning an investigation into whether students who use a phone more spend less time on homework. Write down a suitable hypothesis and state what data Leila needs to collect.
items.answer: Hypothesis, e.g. "Students with more phone time do less homework." Data: daily phone time and daily homework time.

items.stem: Sipho is investigating whether a six-sided dice is biased. Sipho plans to use an experiment rolling the dice many times. Explain whether this will give primary or secondary data, and give one advantage of this method.
items.answer: Primary data. Advantage: collected for exactly this purpose, so it fits the question and you know how it was collected. Disadvantage: it takes time and effort to collect.
items.markingKey: B1 correct type with reason; B1 sensible advantage (and disadvantage). [2]

items.stem: Yusuf says that the height of a sunflower is categorical data. Is Yusuf correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: Daniel wants to investigate how much rain falls in Mumbai in each month. Describe a plan for the investigation. Include (i) a hypothesis, (ii) the data to collect, (iii) how to collect it, (iv) how to present the results.
items.answer: (i) Most rain falls in the middle of the year. (ii) monthly rainfall in mm (iii) weather records from the national weather service, using a sample of a sensible size from months over the last 10 years (iv) a suitable diagram (e.g. bar chart for categories, scatter graph for two measured variables, frequency polygon for grouped data) and averages.

items.markingKey: B1 B1 two valid reasons (time, cost, practicality). [2]

items.stem: A college has 189 Stage 7 students and 356 Stage 8 students. Kenji takes a sample of 50 Stage 7 students and 50 Stage 8 students. Explain why this sample does not represent the college fairly.
items.answer: The groups are different sizes (189 and 356), so taking equal numbers over-represents the smaller group. The sample should be in proportion: about 35 Stage 7 students and 65 Stage 8 students.
items.markingKey: B1 groups different sizes; B1 proportional sizes suggested. [2]

items.stem: A list of 200 customers is numbered 1 to 200. A sample of 20 is taken by choosing a random starting number from 1 to 10 and then every 10th customer. The starting number is 8. Write down the first four customers in the sample, and explain why every customer had the same chance of being chosen.
items.answer: 8, 18, 28, 38. Each starting number from 1 to 10 is equally likely, and each customer belongs to exactly one starting group.
items.markingKey: B1 interval 200 ÷ 20 = 10; B1 four numbers; B1 reason.

items.stem: A school in Istanbul has 32 adults and 72 children. Lucas takes a sample of 26 students in proportion to the size of each group. How many adults and how many children should be in the sample?
items.answer: 8 adults and 18 children

items.stem: A school in Mexico City has 74 full-time workers and 42 part-time workers. Arjun takes a sample of 116 students in proportion to the size of each group. How many full-time workers and how many part-time workers should be in the sample?
items.answer: 74 full-time workers and 42 part-time workers

items.stem: Elena is investigating whether students who use a phone more spend less time on homework. The population is made up of 300 adults and 160 children. (a) Elena wants a sample of 46. Work out how many adults should be in the sample if the groups are represented in proportion. (b) Describe how Elena could choose the adults at random. (c) Elena asks only people who arrive first in the morning. Explain why this sample may be biased.
items.answer: (a) 30 (b) Number the 300 adults; use random numbers to choose the required number, ignoring repeats. (c) Early arrivals may share habits or characteristics; not everyone has an equal chance of selection.

items.stem: Priya asks people at 10 a.m. on a weekday how they travel to work. Why is the sample biased?
options: Many workers are already at work at that time, so the sample misses them.
items.answer: Many workers are already at work at that time, so the sample misses them.
items.markingKey: Many workers are already at work at that time, so the sample misses them. [1]

items.stem: Mateo writes this question for a survey: "Don't you think the new park is a waste of money?" Explain what is wrong with the question.
items.answer: It is a leading question that pushes the person to agree. Better: "What is your opinion of the new park? Very good / Good / Poor / Very poor"
items.markingKey: B1 criticism; B1 improved, neutral question with suitable responses. [2]

items.stem: Ethan writes this question for a survey: "Do you exercise a lot?" Explain what is wrong with the question.
items.answer: "A lot" means different things to different people. Better: "How many hours do you exercise in a typical week? 0 / more than 0 up to 2 / more than 2 up to 4 / more than 4"
items.markingKey: B1 criticism; B1 improved, neutral question with suitable responses. [2]

items.stem: Ravi asks people at a gym how often they exercise, to find out how much exercise people in Muscat do, using the question "Do you exercise a lot?" Describe two different sources of bias in Ravi's survey and explain how to reduce each one.
items.answer: Sample: People at a gym exercise more than average, so the sample is not representative. → Ask a random sample of people from the whole city, e.g. using the electoral list or at several different places and times. Question: "A lot" means different things to different people. → use a neutral question such as "How many hours do you exercise in a typical week? 0 / more than 0 up to 2 / more than 2 up to 4 / more than 4"
items.markingKey: B1 sampling bias; B1 its fix; B1 question bias; B1 its fix. [4]

items.stem: Sofia asks people at a gym how often they exercise, to find out how much exercise people in Cape Town do. Sofia asks 12 people the question "Do you agree that our school canteen serves unhealthy food?" (a) Rewrite the question so that it is not biased. (b) Describe how to choose a better sample.
items.answer: (a) How would you rate the healthiness of the school canteen food? Very healthy / Healthy / Unhealthy / Very unhealthy (b) Ask a random sample of people from the whole city, e.g. using the electoral list or at several different places and times.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 neutral wording; B1 suitable response options [2] (b) B1 B1 [2]

items.stem: A student uses data downloaded from a government website. What type of data is this?
items.answer: Secondary data
items.markingKey: It was collected by someone else. [1]

items.stem: Mateo is investigating how much rain falls in Cairo in each month. Mateo plans to use weather records from the national weather service. Explain whether this will give secondary or primary data, and give one advantage of this method.
items.answer: Secondary data. Advantage: quick and cheap to obtain, often a large amount of data. Disadvantage: it may not be exactly what is needed, may be out of date, and you do not know how carefully it was collected.
items.markingKey: B1 correct type with reason; B1 sensible advantage (and disadvantage). [2]

items.stem: Freya is investigating whether bigger houses in Seoul cost more to rent. Explain why the question "What do you think about it?" would not be a useful question to ask, and suggest a better one.
items.answer: It is vague and will not give data that can be analysed. A better question asks for specific data on floor area and monthly rent, with clear answer options or a number.
items.markingKey: B1 reason (vague / not measurable); B1 improved specific question. [2]

items.stem: Jonas collects the masses of 40 students. The smallest is 30 kg and the largest is 123 kg. Design 5 equal class intervals of width 20 kg for a frequency table, starting at 30 kg.
items.markingKey: B1 correct width and start; B1 classes do not overlap and cover the range (use ≤ x <).

items.stem: Ethan collects the journey times of 40 students. The smallest is 140 minutes and the largest is 160 minutes. Design 5 equal class intervals of width 5 minutes for a frequency table, starting at 140 minutes.
items.markingKey: B1 correct width and start; B1 classes do not overlap and cover the range (use ≤ x <).

items.stem: Kenji collects the masses of 40 students. The smallest is 10 kg and the largest is 111 kg. Design 6 equal class intervals of width 20 kg for a frequency table, starting at 10 kg.
items.markingKey: B1 correct width and start; B1 classes do not overlap and cover the range (use ≤ x <).

items.stem: Yusuf is investigating whether hotter days mean more ice creams are sold at a café in Bangkok. (a) Write a hypothesis for the investigation. (b) State the data that needs to be collected and whether it is primary or secondary. (c) Yusuf uses a sample of size 60. Give one reason why this is better than a sample of size 10.
items.answer: (a) More ice creams are sold on hotter days. (b) daily temperature and number of ice creams sold; secondary data (c) A larger sample is more reliable / representative and reduces the effect of unusual values.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 [1] (b) B1 data; B1 type [2] (c) B1 [1]

items.stem: Leila is investigating how much rain falls in Singapore in each month. (a) Write a hypothesis for the investigation. (b) Leila uses a sample of size 100. Give one reason why this is better than a sample of size 10. (c) Suggest a suitable diagram to display the results and give a reason. (d) Describe one problem that could happen when collecting the data, and how to reduce it.
items.answer: (a) Most rain falls in the middle of the year. (b) A larger sample is more reliable / representative and reduces the effect of unusual values. (c) A time series graph (or a bar chart by month), to show how rainfall changes through the year (d) e.g. people give inaccurate answers / measurements are inaccurate; use clear questions, repeat measurements, use a larger random sample.
items.markingKey: (a) B1 [1] (b) B1 [1] (c) B1 diagram; B1 reason linked to data type [2] (d) B1 problem; B1 solution [2]

items.stem: What usually happens to the results when the size of a random sample is increased?
options: They become exactly the same as the population
items.answer: They become more reliable
items.markingKey: Larger samples reduce the effect of chance variation. [1]

items.stem: Arjun investigates whether people can estimate one minute more accurately with practice, using a sample of 5. Explain why this sample size is not suitable, and suggest a better sample size.
items.answer: A sample of 5 is too small: a few unusual results have a large effect, so it may not represent students in the class. A sample of about 30 to 100 (or more) would be better.
items.markingKey: B1 too small / unrepresentative; B1 sensible larger size or consequence. [2]

items.stem: Explain why a sample that is very large is not always better.
items.answer: It costs more time and money to collect and process; beyond a certain size the extra reliability is small. A large biased sample is still biased.
items.markingKey: B1 cost/time; B1 bias not removed by size. [2]

items.stem: A list of 1200 customers is numbered 1 to 1200. A sample of 25 is taken by choosing a random starting number from 1 to 48 and then every 48th customer. The starting number is 20. Write down the first four customers in the sample, and explain why every customer had the same chance of being chosen.
items.answer: 20, 68, 116, 164. Each starting number from 1 to 48 is equally likely, and each customer belongs to exactly one starting group.
items.markingKey: B1 interval 1200 ÷ 25 = 48; B1 four numbers; B1 reason.

items.stem: A school in Manila has 120 Stage 7 students and 90 Stage 8 students. Lina takes a sample of 7 students in proportion to the size of each group. How many Stage 7 students and how many Stage 8 students should be in the sample?
items.answer: 4 Stage 7 students and 3 Stage 8 students

items.stem: A list of 300 customers is numbered 1 to 300. A sample of 20 is taken by choosing a random starting number from 1 to 15 and then every 15th customer. The starting number is 11. Write down the first four customers in the sample, and explain why every customer had the same chance of being chosen.
items.answer: 11, 26, 41, 56. Each starting number from 1 to 15 is equally likely, and each customer belongs to exactly one starting group.
items.markingKey: B1 interval 300 ÷ 20 = 15; B1 four numbers; B1 reason.

items.stem: Omar is investigating how much rain falls in Muscat in each month. The population is made up of 120 adults and 200 children. (a) Omar wants a sample of 32. Work out how many adults should be in the sample if the groups are represented in proportion. (b) Describe how Omar could choose the adults at random. (c) Explain why a sample of 5 would not be suitable.
items.answer: (a) 12 (b) Number the 120 adults; use random numbers to choose the required number, ignoring repeats. (c) Too small to be representative; results unreliable.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Write down one way to reduce bias when choosing a sample. (b) What is bias in data collection?
items.answer: (a) Choose the sample randomly (and make it large enough). (b) Something that makes the results unrepresentative or unfair in one direction
items.markingKey: (a) B1 [1] (b) Bias distorts results systematically. [1]

items.stem: Explain why response boxes in a questionnaire should not overlap.
items.answer: If they overlap, some answers fit two boxes, so a person could tick either and the results would be unclear.
items.markingKey: B1 values in two boxes; B1 consequence. [2]

items.stem: Daniel asks people at 10 a.m. on a weekday how they travel to work. Explain why Daniel's sample is likely to be biased.
items.answer: Many workers are already at work at that time, so the sample misses them. Improvement: Ask at different times and days, or use a random sample from a list.
items.markingKey: B1 reason for bias; B1 sensible improvement. [2]

items.stem: Samuel surveys people leaving a vegetarian restaurant about their favourite meal, using the question "How much do you spend on lunch?" Describe two different sources of bias in Samuel's survey and explain how to reduce each one.
items.answer: Sample: Vegetarians are over-represented; meat dishes are unlikely to be chosen. → Survey a random sample from the general population. Question: It is vague: no time period, no response boxes. → use a neutral question such as "How much do you usually spend on lunch each day? $0–$2 / more than $2 up to $4 / more than $4 up to $6 / more than $6"
items.markingKey: B1 sampling bias; B1 its fix; B1 question bias; B1 its fix. [4]

items.stem: Hana asks members of a football club which sport is the most popular in the school. Hana asks 12 people the question "Don't you think the new park is a waste of money?" (a) Give two reasons why the results may be biased. (b) Describe how to choose a better sample.
items.answer: (a) Football club members are likely to choose football. Also the question: It is a leading question that pushes the person to agree. (b) Choose a random sample from the whole school register.
